messages.subject: PCA vs PCoA
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

Hoping someone can clear up my PCA / PCoA confusion. I have read the documentation for 'gl.pcoa' https://www.rdocumentation.org/packages/dartR/versions/1.9.9.1/topics/gl.pcoa  (although I have seen posts about bugs and am not sure which dartR version I should be using).

My understanding is that although the function is called ‘gl.pcoa’, it is a wrapper for two separate functions:

If you give it a genlight object, it will use the function ‘glPca’ from ‘Adegenet’ and perform a Pearson Principal Component analysis (PCA), using a Euclidean distance.
If you give it a distance matrix (which can be created via multiple methods) it performs a Gower Principal Coordinate analysis (PCoA) using the function ‘pcoa’ from the ‘Ape’ package.
My data is DArT genlight SNP data and I have been using the following code:
pc <- gl.pcoa(gl)
gl.pcoa.plot(pc, gl)

Therefore I would think that a PCA is produced. My questions are (1) am I indeed performing a PCA, and (2) is this appropriate or should I instead be performing a PCoA?

Thanks in advance!

Kind regards,
Mandi

messages.subject: Re: PCA vs PCoA
messages.body_plain:
Hi Mandi,

The literature is confusing on the distinction between PCA and PCoA (and for that matter MDS).

Basically, PCA takes the original data, for which it is sensible to compute a covariance matrix, and uses that as the basis of the ordination (selecting a new basis in which the axes are ranked on order or variation "explained").

PCoA uses a trick on noting that the analysis does not need access to the raw data except to calculate the cavariance matrix, and so replaces the correlation matrix with any distance matrix (after some transformation) to generate the ordination. For the distances to be accurately represented in the ordinated space, the distance matrix should be Euclidean (else negative eigenvalues are generated), or at the very least a metric distance, but for many purposes, these conditions are not necessary. The resultant distortion in the ordination can be slight, and certainly less than occurs by only considering the top 2 or 3 axes in the ordination.

glPCA uses not the covariance matrix, but Euclidean distance, so depending on how you look at it, it is a PCA or it is a PCoA. Standardized Euclidean distance and the covariance matrix are pretty much the same thing.

With SNP data and gl.pcoa, you are essentially doing a PCA, not a PCoA, and the new version of dartR reflects this in the labelling of the axes. That is fine.

It is only if you wanted to represent genetic distances using some other measure of genetic dissimilarity that you would feed gl.pcoa with a distance matrix directly. You might for example want to feed it the FST's (non-metric), or a fixed difference matrix, or a matrix combining both the SNP genotypes and the SilicoDArT presence absence data, or add in some interval or ordinal data. Then you would use PCoA based on a distance matrix.

I hope that helps. You are doing a PCA.

Arthur

messages.body_plain:
Hi there,

I am using dartR version 1.0.5 because I am using a github script that was written for this version (in case it is important, the github install_github('jdyen/dartR@sexlinkage', dependencies = FALSE, force = TRUE) ).

I have some questions, and hopefully a solution (?) but just want to double check.

1. I would like to filter out minor alleles in a gl created in version 1.0.5. As far as I can see, I can identify minor allele frequency using gl.report.maf(). Is there a way that I can identify them and filter them out?

2. gl.filter.minoralleles() function, in v1.9.9.1, does not work for my genlight object that I created in 1.0.5. It gives me the following error
Error in if (x@other$loc.metrics.flags$monomorphs == FALSE) { :
  argument is of length zero

3. In the error above, gl.filter.minoralleles() from version 1.9.9.1 appears to be looking for monomorphs (i.e. $monomorphs). In which case, can I use gl.filter.monomorphs() from 1.0.5? Are these two functions doing the same thing?

Many thanks!
Lana

messages.subject: Re: [dartR] Missing Data in PCoA
messages.body_plain:
Hi Dallas,

PCA does not like missing data. The algorithm as initially developed by Pearson expects a complete dataset.

Algorithms treat missing data in different ways. As I understand it, a common approach is to replace the missing element with the central value which, because PCA has no advance knowledge of group membership, can be problematic if the objective of the analysis is to identify groupings. Only matters where missing data is fairly extreme. An alternative with SNPs is to replace the missing data with a random selection of the two possible SNP states. This throws in an additional element of noise which would not distort the outcome. I am not sure what {adegenet} glPCA does. It is at the heart of our script. I expect it is something along the lines of the latter.

The distances computed for PCA are Euclidean, which means they can be represented in a rigid (cartesian) space without distortion provided the ordination has the full set of dimensions. I believe missing data depending on how they are handled, can destroy the Euclidean property, and can therefore result in distortion and even negative eigenvalues. But again, the level of missing data would need to be extreme to cause this.

With PCoA, where the starting point is a distance matrix, it will depend on how the distance measure accommodates missing values. You do not get something for nothing, so a distance matrix calculated with a Euclidean distance from data with missing values will likely no longer satisfy the Euclidean properties, if that is important.

Missing values in the distance matrix itself should be avoided, as PCOA does not access the original SNP data and so needs to fill in the missing value using some central value approach.

If I had a magic wand, I would take advantage of my prior knowledge of populations that contributed to the dataset, assume HWE for each population (sampling site), and replace the missing values by substituting a SNP score (0, 1 or 2) with a value consistent with expectation under HWE. That will add random noise to the dataset which, if extreme for any one locus, will push its contribution down to lower dimensions in the ordination and not influence the outcome in the one, two or three dimensions of the final visual outcome.

Perhaps this is something we could add to version 2 of dartR after it is released shortly?

I should add that I am not an expert in this and if someone with a deeper mathematical knowledge would like to contribute that would be great. Even if you contradict my interpretation, I won't be offended.

Hope this helps Dallas.

Arthur

messages.subject: When to check for HWE
messages.body_plain:
Generally if one has a collection of SNPs from a number of animals, in screening for an analysis one would check for HWE.  But let's say these animals were a collection from a number of different locations so they might have slightly different population SNP patterns or if they were a collection of captive animals.  In such cases is it truly reasonable to expect HWE and so should one skip doing a check on HWE in preparing the data for analysis?

Janice Boyd
Texas A&M

messages.subject: Re: [dartR] When to check for HWE
messages.body_plain:
Hi Janice,

Testing for HWE is falls into that difficult class of statistical analyses where the conclusion and resultant action depends on failure to reject a null hypothesis. "We tested for HWE and found no statistically significant departures". The trouble with that statement is that the finding is ambiguous -- there might be no actual departures from HWE or there might be quite substantial departures but not statistically significant because of low sample sizes. If you really wanted to hang you hat on a conclusion that a particular population is in HWE, you would need to do a power analysis to show that it was reasonable to conclude that the sample sizes were adequate to detect a departure from HWE of consequence were it to exist. So I tend to do what you have said, that is, that given the low sample sizes, only gross departures from HWE could be detected; however, none were so we assumed HWE for all sampled populations. Something like that.

It there are a lot of populations, or if you are testing for departure of HWE for loci, then you have the issue of compounding error to contend with. With low sample sizes the power to identify loci out of HWE is very challenging. You are probably best to say something like "Given the low within-population sample sizes (n < 12, say), we did not filter loci for departures from Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium (HWE) or linkage disequilibrium".

The other point you make is true also. If you apply HWE as a null hypothesis when considering multiple populations, then rejection of the null hypothesis is an indication of genetic structure across those populations, not an indication that any one of them is out of HWE. Like saying, are these isolated or semi-isolated populations, when the data are pooled, out of HWE -- well, duh! The issue then arises of power. Depending on the sample sizes, which may vary, failure to demonstrate a significant departure from HWE does not mean the populations from which the samples are taken do not depart substantially from HWE. When you demonstrate departure from HWE, despite low sample sizes, then it can be taken as an indication of structure across populations, but this is embedded in a background of undetected and possibly substantial structure arising from failure to reject the null hypothesis because of low and variable sample sizes.

I hope this helps. Others may have contrary views.

Arthur

messages.body_plain:
Thank you, Dr Gruber.  Your comments have strengthened my feelings that, if I am doing a screening (before actual analysis) of a SNP dataset from captive populations or wild populations from a variety of locations, then there is no real justification/reason for throwing out SNPS that fail a HWE test.  In fact, such a screen would mostly be just to see if anything grossly surprising occurs that prompts an examination of the whole sequencing and SNP extraction steps.

If anyone on this list thinks I am not correct,please let me know.

Thanks.

Janice Boyd
Texas A&M

messages.subject: Re: [dartR] When to check for HWE
messages.body_plain:
I would chime in and say that the question matters. For example, if you were doing a fixed difference test, you would expect the populations to not be in HWE. Fixed differences only arise because of HWE violations. If you get significant fixed differences, you then need to think about what HWE assumptions are being violated. If the population is large and generally continuous, maybe different species. If it’s a captive population, probably small and not randomly mating. If it’s declining and fragmented, probably that’s the fixed difference cause. Also a pet peeve of mine as a reviewer - people finding fixed differences in anthropogenically fragmented declining species and thinking they are different species, instead of attributing the lack of HWE to genetic drift and lack of random mating.

The lack of HWE can be really informative about what is happening to a population in some circumstances.

Rant over!

Renee
